articles.title: CMA CGM announces new Asia–Mediterranean rates and Mozambique surcharge
articles.summary: CMA CGM has announced new Freight All Kinds (FAK) rates from Asia to the Mediterranean and North Africa, alongside a revised Peak Season Surcharge (PSS) for shipments from South China to Mozambique. The updated FAK rates will apply from 1 to 14 December 2026, while the Mozambique surcharge took effect on 15 November....
articles.body: CMA CGM has announced new Freight All Kinds (FAK) rates from Asia to the Mediterranean and North Africa, alongside a revised Peak Season Surcharge (PSS) for shipments from South China to Mozambique. The updated FAK rates will apply from 1 to 14 December 2026, while the Mozambique surcharge took effect on 15 November. New FAK rates for Asia–Mediterranean shipments CMA CGM has increased its FAK rates for shipments from all main Asian ports to destinations across the Mediterranean, Black Sea and North Africa. For the West Mediterranean, rates have been set at US$5,300 per 20-foot container and US$6,600 per 40-foot or 40-foot high-cube container. The Adriatic will see rates of US$5,400 and US$6,700, respectively, while East Mediterranean shipments will be charged US$5,500 for 20-foot containers and US$6,800 for 40-foot equipment. For the Black Sea, the carrier has announced rates of US$5,600 per 20-foot container and US$6,900 per 40-foot container. North Africa will face the highest rates, reaching US$6,400 for 20-foot containers and US$8,800 for 40-foot or high-cube equipment. The new rates cover dry containers, refrigerated cargo, out-of-gauge shipments and paying empty containers. According to CMA CGM, the announced FAK rates include basic ocean freight, bunker-related surcharges, EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) charges and Low Sulphur Surcharge (LSS). Terminal handling charges, safety and security fees, and other applicable local or contingency charges may be added. South China–Mozambique surcharge revised Separately, CMA CGM has revised its Peak Season Surcharge for shipments from South China to Mozambique. The new charge is US$300 per TEU, effective from 15 November 2026 until further notice. The adjustment represents a reduction of US$100 per TEU compared with the previously announced surcharge of US$400 per TEU, which had applied from 10 November. The revised PSS applies to all cargo types and is charged separately from the applicable basic ocean freight rate. Additional bunker-related, terminal handling, safety and security, and local charges may also apply. The two announcements reflect further adjustments to CMA CGM’s pricing across its Asia–Mediterranean and Asia–Africa trade networks ahead of December.

articles.title: Shipping heavyweights warn against double carbon charges
articles.summary: Nine of the world’s leading shipping associations have joined forces to push governments towards a global emissions deal, warning that a patchwork of regional regulations risks leaving shipowners paying multiple times for the same carbon emissions. The joint intervention comes ahead of a crucial round of talks at the...
articles.body: Environment Operations Regulatory Shipping heavyweights warn against double carbon charges Adis Ajdin November 18, 2026 0 27 2 minutes read IMO IMO Nine of the world’s leading shipping associations have joined forces to push governments towards a global emissions deal, warning that a patchwork of regional regulations risks leaving shipowners paying multiple times for the same carbon emissions. The joint intervention comes ahead of a crucial round of talks at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) later this month, with governments still divided over how to regulate and price shipping’s greenhouse gas emissions. BIMCO, the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), Intercargo, Intertanko, the World Shipping Council, Cruise Lines International Association (CLIA), Interferry, the International Bunker Industry Association (IBIA) and the International Parcel Tankers Association (IPTA) have called for a single global framework that applies equally to vessels regardless of flag, ownership or trade. “Shipping is a global industry requiring global rules applied equally to all ships,” the organisations said. The groups warned that national and regional schemes could result in duplicated compliance requirements and multiple charges for the same emissions, undermining efforts to establish a level playing field. They want an IMO agreement that rewards verifiable emissions reductions while giving shipowners sufficient flexibility to manage the transition to cleaner fuels, many of which remain commercially unavailable for much of the existing fleet. The joint statement also calls for regulations that are fuel- and technology-neutral, enforceable and backed by clear incentives for investment in alternative fuels and energy-saving technologies. The intervention comes after the IMO failed to secure agreement on its proposed Net-Zero Framework in October 2025, forcing governments to postpone adoption for a year. The framework, which combines a global marine fuel standard with an emissions-pricing mechanism, remains the subject of negotiations over its cost, design and implementation. The industry’s latest appeal follows growing concern over the spread of regional carbon schemes. Several African governments are moving towards their own shipping emissions charges, while European operators already face the EU Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime regulations. The nine associations warned that the lack of regulatory certainty is complicating investment decisions for shipowners, ports, fuel producers and financiers, particularly given the limited availability and high cost of lower-emissions fuels. Governments will resume negotiations at the IMO’s greenhouse gas working group from November 23 to 27, followed by the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s 85th session from November 30 to December 3. A further extraordinary session to consider adoption of the emissions framework could take place on December 4, subject to confirmation during MEPC 85. articles.title: DEME orders pair of autonomous offshore survey vessels
articles.summary: Belgian marine contractor DEME has ordered two uncrewed offshore survey vessels from Dutch technology specialist DEMCON Unmanned Systems, expanding its capabilities in remote and autonomous offshore operations. The vessels will be based on DEMCON’s DUS OV platform, which incorporates a DNV type-approved design and...
articles.body: Europe Offshore Renewables DEME orders pair of autonomous offshore survey vessels Bojan Lepic November 18, 2026 0 62 1 minute read DEMCON DEMCON Belgian marine contractor DEME has ordered two uncrewed offshore survey vessels from Dutch technology specialist DEMCON Unmanned Systems, expanding its capabilities in remote and autonomous offshore operations. The vessels will be based on DEMCON’s DUS OV platform, which incorporates a DNV type-approved design and technology intended to support certification for autonomous operations. The two units are already under construction, with delivery scheduled for 2027. Designed for multi-day offshore deployment, the vessels can operate directly from ports or be launched from larger offshore construction vessels. Their modular construction allows them to be transported internationally in standard shipping containers, providing flexibility when mobilising for survey campaigns. The contract also includes launch-and-recovery equipment, vessel-handling systems, and the integration of DEME’s survey instruments and communications technology. The new vessels will be equipped with DEMCON’s autonomous navigation and mission management software, supporting survey-route following, collision avoidance, dynamic positioning and remote intervention. A dedicated remote operations centre will allow personnel to monitor vessel systems, navigation, survey equipment, and operational performance. The design incorporates redundant propulsion, power, navigation and communication systems to maintain control in the event of individual equipment failures. DEMCON said the vessels were being developed in response to increasing demand for remote survey operations across offshore wind and marine infrastructure projects. The two companies are currently undertaking detailed engineering and systems integration work ahead of testing and delivery next year. articles.body: Containers Dry Cargo Greater China CSSC Shipping adds two bulkers and takes over ASL boxship pair Adis Ajdin November 18, 2026 0 92 1 minute read Hong Kong-listed CSSC Shipping has signed up for another two 80,000 dwt grain carriers in China while moving to take over a pair of containership newbuildings from ASL Shipping in a combined HK$1.73bn ($221m) transaction. The ship leasing arm of state-owned China Shipbuilding Group has entered into two new contracts with Chengxi Shipyard and China Shipbuilding Trading, with Chengxi and CSSC Guangxi jointly responsible for building the vessels. Each bulker is priced at CNH326m ($49.3m), putting the latest two-ship commitment at CNH652m ($98.6m). The vessels are scheduled for completion by the end of 2029 and 2030, respectively. The fresh orders come just over two months after CSSC Shipping signed for ten 80,000 dwt bulkers at the same shipbuilding group in a CNH3.235bn ($481m) deal. The additional pair takes the company’s grain carrier programme to 12 vessels, subject to the necessary approvals. Alongside the bulker contracts, CSSC Shipping has agreed to shift two existing 5,300 teu containership orders at Guangzhou Wenchong into CA Shipping, its joint venture with ASL Navigation. The vessels were originally contracted by ASL Shipping . Under novation agreements, CA Shipping will assume the original buyer’s rights and obligations. The contracts are worth $61.4m per ship, or $122.8m combined, with construction scheduled for completion in September and November 2028. CA Shipping is 60% owned by CSSC Shipping subsidiary Fortune Vcontainer Carriers, with the remaining 40% held by ASL Navigation, a subsidiary of ASL Shipping. Both transactions remain subject to independent shareholder approval and the effectiveness of the associated bareboat charter agreements. If the containership novations fail to take effect by January 31, 2027, the original contracts will remain with ASL Shipping. CSSC Shipping said it plans to finance the package through internal resources and bank borrowings, with the vessels intended to generate leasing income. articles.title: Guinea Leaps to Third-largest Iron Ore Exporter
articles.summary: "In October 2026, Guinea became the world’s third-largest iron ore exporter, with exports surpassing 5m tonnes for the first time and accounting for 3% of global iron ore volumes. The country has gradually ramped up shipments following the start of mining operations at Simandou in December 2025.
articles.body: Guinea Leaps to Third-largest Iron Ore Exporter Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 18, 2026 Chart courtesy BIMCO "In October 2026, Guinea became the world’s third-largest iron ore exporter, with exports surpassing 5m tonnes for the first time and accounting for 3% of global iron ore volumes. The country has gradually ramped up shipments following the start of mining operations at Simandou in December 2025. More than 22m tonnes have been shipped so far in 2026, already surpassing initial industry projections of around 20m tonnes for the full year,” says Filipe Gouveia, Shipping Analysis Manager at BIMCO. The Simandou mining project is in southeastern Guinea and contains one of the world’s largest deposits of high-grade iron ore. Once fully ramped up, the project is expected to have an annual capacity of around 120m tonnes, equivalent to an average of 10m tonnes per month. With exports surpassing 5m tonnes in October, Guinea has already reached around half of Simandou’s planned monthly capacity. Full capacity is projected to be reached towards the end of the decade, although the exact timescale remains uncertain. “Guinean iron ore exports are particularly beneficial for ship demand, as they typically travel 88% longer distances than the average iron ore shipment. Consequently, the exports accounted for 6% of global iron ore tonne-mile demand in October. Overall, the increase in Guinean shipments contributed to a 2% y/y increase in global iron ore tonne miles between January and October, despite stagnant cargo volumes,” says Gouveia. Guinean iron ore has headed almost exclusively to China, the world’s largest iron ore importer. China relies on a combination of high-grade imported iron ore and domestic supplies, which are often of a lower grade, to supply its steel industry. So far this year, China’s steel production has fallen 3% y/y due to weaker demand, while iron ore shipments to the country have risen 1% y/y. Growing supply from major exporters, including Guinea, has weighed on iron ore prices, making imported ore increasingly competitive with domestic Chinese mining. At the same time, lower prices have intensified competition among exporters, prompting some smaller Brazilian miners to reduce output amid weaker prices and high freight costs. “Simandou could have a significant impact on capesize ship demand, even if its exports partly displace existing iron ore trade. Global iron ore tonne-mile demand could rise 13% compared with 2025 if Guinean exports reach 120m tonnes while other exporters maintain their volumes. Even if every additional Guinean tonne replaces an existing shipment, the longer sailing distances could still increase tonne-mile demand by around 6%,” says Gouveia.

articles.body: Africa Americas Europe Offshore Saipem bags drilling double in Egypt and Suriname Bojan Lepic November 18, 2026 0 82 1 minute read Saipem Saipem Italian offshore engineering and drilling contractor Saipem has secured two new contracts worth approximately $181m for its Scarabeo 9 semisubmersible drilling rig. Burullus Gas Company, a joint venture between Shell, Petronas, and the Egyptian state-owned Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation (EGPC), awarded the first contract. The agreement covers the drilling of three offshore wells in Egypt, with operations scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2027. The second award comes from TotalEnergies EP Suriname and covers five firm wells, with options for another five. The campaign will begin following completion of the Egyptian assignment. Saipem did not disclose the individual contract values or identify the specific fields involved. Burullus operates the West Delta Deep Marine concession offshore Egypt, where Shell and its partners sanctioned the three-well Phase 12a development in August. First gas from that project is expected in 2028. Meanwhile, TotalEnergies is progressing its $10.5bn GranMorgu oil development offshore Suriname, where drilling and installation activities are scheduled to ramp up in 2027 ahead of first oil in 2028. The latest awards follow two drilling contracts worth $121m that Saipem announced in October. As Splash previously reported, those agreements included work for Scarabeo 9 offshore Ghana and a separate campaign for the Saipem 10000 drillship offshore Cyprus. Saipem said the latest awards would strengthen its drilling backlog and provide greater visibility on the rig’s utilisation throughout 2027 and 2028. articles.title: Sallaum Logistics opens new inland vehicle hub in Belgium
articles.summary: Sallaum Logistics has announced the opening of a 57,000-square-metre customs-bonded vehicle compound at the Port of Limburg in Genk, Belgium, extending its logistics operations beyond the Port of Antwerp. The new facility provides additional inland storage and customs-handling capacity for finished vehicles. It also...
articles.body: Sallaum Logistics has announced the opening of a 57,000-square-metre customs-bonded vehicle compound at the Port of Limburg in Genk, Belgium, extending its logistics operations beyond the Port of Antwerp. The new facility provides additional inland storage and customs-handling capacity for finished vehicles. It also allows customers to move cargo from Antwerp to Genk before completing import procedures. Located along the Albert Canal, the compound offers access to inland waterways, rail and road transport. Its position near the Dutch and German borders also supports vehicle distribution across neighbouring European markets. New facility connects Antwerp with inland transport networks The Genk compound provides a barge connection to Antwerp and access to railway infrastructure capable of handling two block trains simultaneously. Sallaum Logistics will also use its road transport fleet to support deliveries between ports, manufacturing facilities, storage locations and customers. The facility is scheduled to open during November 2026 and will operate as part of the company’s wider European vehicle logistics network. Under the customs-bonded arrangement, vehicles can be transferred from Antwerp to Genk while remaining under customs control. Import duties remain suspended while vehicles are stored under bond, with customs clearance completed in Genk when customers are ready to receive their cargo. According to Sallaum Logistics, the arrangement will help reduce pressure on terminal space in Antwerp. It will also allow importers and manufacturers to coordinate vehicle deliveries with production schedules, dealership requirements and customer demand. “The opening of our Genk Port Customs bonded compound represents an important step in strengthening our integrated logistics network across Europe,” said Edvinas Rybelis, CEO, Sallaum Logistics. Rybelis also highlighted the potential for rail and inland waterways to support more efficient and lower-emission transport operations. The new site extends the company’s existing logistics chain, which combines Sallaum Lines’ maritime vehicle transport operations with terminal handling in Antwerp and inland distribution services. Customers already using the Antwerp terminal will be able to route vehicles through Genk without changing their logistics provider or existing contractual arrangements, according to the company. The development follows the launch of Sallaum Logistics as a dedicated European automotive logistics business earlier this year.

articles.title: UK sets out 2030 marine fuel crackdown
articles.summary: Britain has laid out plans for a new shipping fuel regulation that could initially cover around 5,000 vessels calling at its ports, including ships operating on international routes. The Department for Transport opened a consultation this week on a proposed greenhouse gas intensity standard, which the government...
articles.body: Bunkering Environment Europe Operations Regulatory UK sets out 2030 marine fuel crackdown Adis Ajdin November 18, 2026 0 181 1 minute read UK Government UK Government Britain has laid out plans for a new shipping fuel regulation that could initially cover around 5,000 vessels calling at its ports, including ships operating on international routes. The Department for Transport opened a consultation this week on a proposed greenhouse gas intensity standard, which the government expects to introduce from 2030. The regime would initially apply to ships of 5,000 gt and above, irrespective of flag, requiring operators to progressively reduce the lifecycle emissions intensity of the fuels and energy they use. Under the government’s preferred approach, the rules would cover all energy consumed on domestic voyages, half the energy used on voyages between British and foreign ports, and emissions generated while ships are alongside in the UK. The obligation would fall on shipping companies rather than bunker suppliers. Britain is taking its lead from the EU’s FuelEU Maritime framework, which entered into force in January 2025, while seeking to retain flexibility around future IMO requirements. Government modelling suggests 4,913 vessels of at least 5,000 gt called at UK ports in 2019. Another 2,405 smaller ships could eventually be brought into the regime if the threshold is lowered to 400 gt. The consultation leaves several important questions unresolved, including how quickly emissions limits should tighten, how operators could pool or trade compliance credits, and the penalties for missing targets. The latest move comes after domestic shipping was brought into the UK Emissions Trading Scheme in July. British shipowners have already warned against copying the administrative problems encountered under FuelEU Maritime. In October, the UK Chamber of Shipping called for better-aligned reporting systems and realistic targets reflecting the availability of alternative fuels. The consultation closes on February 22, 2027. articles.summary: The U.S. Coast Guard's largest icebreaker, USCGC Healy, suffered a catastrophic overspeed failure of one of its main propulsion diesel generators in July, triggering a fire in the generator room and requiring extensive repairs to electrical and fire-detection systems, and corrective maintenance affecting two...

The U.S. Coast Guard’s largest icebreaker, USCGC Healy , suffered a catastrophic overspeed failure of one of its main propulsion diesel generators in July, triggering a fire in the generator room and requiring extensive repairs to electrical and fire-detection systems, and corrective maintenance affecting two additional engines, according to Coast Guard procurement documents. The documents provide the most detailed account yet of the incident aboard the 420-foot icebreaker, which was towed back to its homeport in Seattle on July 13 after experiencing a significant engineering casualty while operating northwest of Port Angeles, Washington . The Coast Guard announced the incident on July 24, saying Healy would undergo major repairs and an investigation. The vessel subsequently abandoned its planned 2026 high-latitude summer mission . The decision to end icebreaker Healy ’s planned high-latitude mission left the service leaning more heavily on its newest icebreaker during an increasingly active Arctic season . A procurement document issued in October for corrective maintenance on two of Healy ‘s other main propulsion diesel generators provides a more specific description of the incident, stating: “CGC HEALY suffered a catastrophic overspeed failure of its #2 MPDG.” The document also recommended immediate corrective action on the overspeed protection devices and governor equipment on generators No. 1 and No. 3. A separate September procurement document for an overhaul of Healy ‘s fire-detection system describes a subsequent fire in Generator Room No. 2 and the resulting damage. “The USCGC HEALY experienced an engine casualty in Generator Room #2 that resulted in a fire in the compartment,” the document states. “Fire detection equipment and wiring were exposed to high temperatures causing a ground fault in the system.” The document continues that “all equipment and wiring in the upper section of the Generator room will need to be renewed.” The fire also caused numerous faults in the detection system, while its Person Machine Interface (PMI-2) was experiencing problems retaining memory and required replacement. The Coast Guard sought a contractor to overhaul the Siemens FireFinder XLS system, including replacement of damaged detection equipment and wiring. The work was to be performed alongside at Coast Guard Base Seattle, with a completion deadline of October 16. The October solicitation provides further insight into the maintenance required following the failure of generator No. 2. The Coast Guard sought contractors to overhaul the mechanical and electro-pneumatic overspeed protection systems on generators No. 1 and No. 3, as well as their Woodward governors and associated equipment. The work included disassembly, inspection, cleaning, repair, recalibration and bench testing of the mechanical overspeed cutouts and electro-pneumatic limiters. The governors and their boosters were also to be removed, completely disassembled, inspected against original equipment manufacturer specifications, fitted with replacement seals and bearings, and bench tested. The solicitation contained another revealing detail about the condition of the machinery. “The governors and boosters appeared to be operating properly but there is no record of service or overhaul,” the document states. It adds that both engines had accumulated more than 40,000 operating hours. The work also included replacement of the A2 cylinder head on engine No. 3 because of damage to the dummy-valve seating surface and dummy-valve body. The removed cylinder head and valve were to be sent to a machine shop for inspection and reconditioning. The Coast Guard scheduled the corrective maintenance between October 13 and October 31 in Seattle. The contract also included an option for up to $60,000 in additional repairs if inspections identified further problems. Meanwhile, a separate procurement addressed the vessel’s CO2 fire-suppression system, including replacement of manual fire-pull equipment and associated cabling serving Generator Rooms No. 1 and No. 2. The documents do not establish whether all the contracted work has been completed or provide a revised return-to-service date for the icebreaker. Another procurement published November 13 provides a glimpse of the Coast Guard’s longer-term maintenance plans for Healy ‘s integrated propulsion plant. The Surface Forces Logistics Center is conducting market research for a five-year support requirement covering July 2028 through July 2033. The proposed contract would cover maintenance and technical support for the vessel’s integrated machinery plant and associated shoreside equipment. GE Power Conversion, part of GE Vernova, is identified as the original equipment manufacturer and holder of the proprietary data rights needed to provide the support. The previous contract was awarded to GE on a sole-source basis. The proposed scope includes periodic equipment maintenance, technical support and troubleshooting, casualty response, engineering analysis, configuration management, and replacement of obsolete components. It also specifically calls for hands-on and classroom training for both Healy ‘s permanent crew and Coast Guard shore-support personnel. The requirement includes evaluating equipment obsolescence and forecasting reliability, maintainability and availability concerns five years beyond the contract period. It also calls for technical upgrades intended to maintain operational availability through the vessel’s midlife maintenance period. The November notice is a sources-sought market survey rather than a request for proposals or an awarded contract. It does not establish that the long-term support arrangement is a consequence of the July casualty. The Coast Guard has not publicly released the findings of its investigation into the overspeed failure or provided a detailed repair timeline. It did not respond to a request for comment. Whether Healy will be ready to resume Arctic operations for the 2027 navigation season remains unclear. articles.summary: Oil is increasingly moving through the Strait of Hormuz on smaller vessels, helping sustain exports as attacks on supertankers squeeze availability of the ships that typically dominate the trade.

REUTERS/Amr Alfiky/File Photo By Weilun Soon Nov 18, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Oil is increasingly moving through the Strait of Hormuz on smaller vessels, helping sustain exports as attacks on supertankers squeeze availability of the ships that typically dominate the trade. The volume shipped through the waterway by Suezmaxes and Aframaxes has climbed over the past two months, hitting a wartime high of more than 2 million barrels a day in October, according to Vortexa. That helped elevate overall daily exports to 11.4 million barrels, the highest since the conflict began. The lucrative but risky trade of shuttling crude out of the Persian Gulf during the US-Iran war has primarily relied on very large crude carriers, which can carry up to 2 million barrels. The supertankers account for 72% of the vessels transiting Hormuz, according to BRS Shipbrokers, although they have become the target of Iranian attacks, taking some out of operation. The use of Suezmaxes and Aframaxes has helped ensure Gulf exports remain robust, according to shipbrokers and traders. The vessels, which carry less than half as much as a VLCC, have mostly been used to load cargoes from Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar, they said. The tankers either transfer crude to other ships after passing through Hormuz or sail directly to ports, often in India. The Lucia A is among the first Suezmaxes to enter the trade, ship-tracking data show. Since June, it’s picked up at least four cargoes from Iraq and delivered them to ships waiting in the Gulf of Oman or to Ain Sukhna, an Egyptian port in the Red Sea. Earlier this month, it loaded its fifth Iraqi shipment. Another Suezmax, the Ture, collected its third Iraqi cargo last week, according to ship-tracking data. The vessel previously transported crude from Russia’s western ports to India, a trade permitted as long as the oil complies with price-cap guidelines imposed by the Group of Seven nations. An attempt to contact the Marshall Islands-based owner of Lucia A was unsuccessful. The ship’s safety manager in Shanghai and the manager of Ture in Greece, did not immediately respond to emailed requests for comment. Smaller vessels also offer significantly lower freight costs. While they carry less crude, supertanker rates have risen much faster than those for other tankers since the start of the war. Shipbrokers have assessed the rate for a Suezmax traveling from the Persian Gulf to China at around a third to just under half the published benchmark rate for a VLCC on the same route. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: Hafnia abandons Torm merger push and heads for exit
articles.summary: BW Group-backed Hafnia has abandoned its pursuit of Danish product tanker rival Torm and is preparing to unwind its near-20% holding after failing to win support for a combination of the two shipping giants. The Oslo- and New York-listed owner said on Wednesday it intends to exit its entire 19.85% stake, preferably...
articles.body: Asia Europe Tankers Hafnia abandons Torm merger push and heads for exit Adis Ajdin November 18, 2026 0 570 2 minutes read TORM TORM BW Group-backed Hafnia has abandoned its pursuit of Danish product tanker rival Torm and is preparing to unwind its near-20% holding after failing to win support for a combination of the two shipping giants. The Oslo- and New York-listed owner said on Wednesday it intends to exit its entire 19.85% stake, preferably by distributing its 20.36m Torm shares to Hafnia shareholders through a special dividend. The holding was valued at $686.6m based on Torm’s November 17 closing share price of $33.73.The move brings an abrupt end to a consolidation push that saw Hafnia spend more than $500m building its position in Torm over the past year. Chief executive Søren Steenberg Jensen confirmed the change of course in the company’s third-quarter results, saying its attempts to engage with Torm had gone nowhere. “Our approaches to Torm have not been reciprocated,” Jensen said, adding that further resistance would diminish the potential benefits of combining the two companies. Hafnia said it would instead pursue other growth and consolidation opportunities. Under the proposed exit, Hafnia shareholders would receive one Torm share for every 26.3 Hafnia shares held, with fractional entitlements settled in cash. The distribution, worth approximately $1.28 per Hafnia share at Tuesday’s closing price, would replace the company’s regular cash dividends for the third and fourth quarters. The plan is not yet final. Hafnia said it needs cooperation from third parties to complete the transaction and has set November 25 as the deadline. If that cannot be secured, the company intends to pay a conventional cash dividend equivalent to 90% of third-quarter net profit instead. Hafnia began building its position in September 2025 when it struck a deal with Oaktree Capital Management to acquire around 14.16m Torm shares for $311.4m, at $22 apiece. The transaction was completed in December, giving Hafnia a stake of just under 14%. The company stepped up its buying in September this year, paying $145.1m for another 4.5m shares before adding a further 1.7m shares for $57.8m. Those purchases took its holding to 19.85% and made Hafnia Torm’s largest disclosed shareholder. Hafnia also raised $300m through a share placement in September to strengthen its balance sheet following the purchases and provide funding for potential strategic opportunities. Across the three disclosed acquisitions, the company spent approximately $514m assembling the Torm stake, which has since risen substantially in market value. While the merger ambitions have been shelved, Hafnia is pressing ahead with its own fleet investments. The company said it plans to exercise purchase options on eight vessels worth around $235m over the coming quarters. articles.body: Dry Cargo Europe Operations Kerch bridge collapse threatens Azov grain trade Sam Chambers November 18, 2026 0 452 1 minute read X.com X.com The partial collapse of the Kerch Strait Bridge following Ukrainian strikes could delay the reopening of one of Russia’s most important grain export routes by months, as the war’s maritime infrastructure battle intensifies. Ukraine destroyed a central road span of the bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea on Tuesday, with debris falling into the Kerch-Yenikale Canal, the only navigable passage connecting the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea. The railway section was also damaged, although Russian authorities subsequently reported the resumption of limited train services. Andrey Sizov, managing director of Russian agricultural consultancy SovEcon, warned that removing the collapsed structure could substantially delay any eventual resumption of commercial shipping. The Sea of Azov normally accounts for approximately 25% of Russian grain exports, according to SovEcon, but shipping through the strait has been suspended since July following repeated drone attacks. Until now, much of the region’s export infrastructure had escaped serious damage, potentially allowing traffic to resume relatively quickly if security conditions improved. The collapsed bridge presents a different challenge, requiring substantial engineering work before deepsea navigation can safely restart. No official timetable for clearing the channel has been confirmed. The latest developments come amid another escalation in attacks on commercial shipping and energy infrastructure. Russia’s defence ministry claimed on Wednesday morning that its forces had struck port infrastructure at Izmail on the Danube and an unnamed general cargo ship sailing towards Pivdennyi, allegedly carrying dual-use military supplies. Moscow provided no vessel identification, casualty figures or independently verifiable damage assessment. The claims have not been independently confirmed. Ukrainian officials separately reported Russian strikes on energy infrastructure in southern Odesa region, leaving parts of Izmail without electricity. Meanwhile, Ukrainian drones struck the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat refinery in Bashkortostan on Tuesday, targeting a complex capable of processing approximately 10m tonnes of oil annually. articles.title: Andre Simha: Shipping needs to fix its foundations before chasing AI
articles.summary: Shipping companies risk pouring money into artificial intelligence before fixing the poor data and disconnected systems that continue to hold back the industry, according to former MSC digital chief André Simha. After four decades with the world’s largest container shipping line, Simha has moved into advising...
articles.body: Maritime CEO Operations Tech Andre Simha: Shipping needs to fix its foundations before chasing AI Splash November 18, 2026 0 273 4 minutes read MSC MSC Shipping companies risk pouring money into artificial intelligence before fixing the poor data and disconnected systems that continue to hold back the industry, according to former MSC digital chief André Simha. After four decades with the world’s largest container shipping line, Simha has moved into advising maritime technology investors, incubators and startups. He sees plenty of opportunities for new technology but warns that shipping’s appetite for AI could run ahead of its ability to put it to good use. “I like to think of AI as a very fast, very confident new colleague,” he tells Maritime CEO. “If you give that colleague bad data, you get bad answers, only faster and with better presentation.” Simha recalls a meeting in Valencia where everyone wanted predictive analytics, but nobody could agree on what constituted a vessel’s departure. Carriers, terminals and rail operators were all working with different definitions of the same event. Technology doesn’t fix a broken process “You can’t build a reliable prediction on top of that,” he argues. He sees the strongest commercial returns from AI coming through document processing, exception handling, more accurate estimated arrival times, customer service, predictive maintenance and fuel and routing optimisation. Fully autonomous decision-making is another matter. “It makes good headlines, but I’d want to see the data underneath first.” The same thinking is shaping his work with maritime technology startups and investors following his departure from MSC in March this year. Rather than replacing existing systems, Simha favours technologies that improve connectivity, clean up data and allow carriers, ports and terminals to work from the same information. He is particularly wary of startups developing solutions without first establishing whether customers have a problem worth solving. “One mistake I see is starting with the technology and searching for a problem. Find the use case first, then the technology,” he explains. Another recurring problem is the failure to turn successful trials into commercially viable products. Shipping’s lengthy sales cycles, integration requirements and reluctance to change are often underestimated. “As I often say to founders, technology doesn’t fix a broken process.” Few areas illustrate that problem better than the industry’s long-running effort to eliminate paper bills of lading. Simha played a leading role in establishing the Digital Container Shipping Association (DCSA) in 2019 and chaired its supervisory board until March 2026. Its carrier members have committed to issuing 100% electronic bills of lading (eBLs) by 2030, an ambition he still considers achievable, although far from certain. “Ambitious, but I’d call it a stretch rather than a fantasy.” He maintains that the technology is no longer the obstacle. Electronic bills of lading are already available, but their wider adoption depends on banks, cargo owners and regulators accepting them throughout the entire transaction. A carrier can issue an electronic document, but the process falls apart if a bank financing the shipment or a customs authority at the destination still insists on paper. “Banks are right to be careful, because they carry the risk, but they now need to move from ‘we’re studying it’ to ‘we accept it’.” Simha also wants regulators to give electronic documents the same legal standing as paper and cargo owners to make eBLs a standard contractual requirement. He argues that the next breakthrough will come from complete trade flows involving every participant, rather than isolated digital transactions. Similar obstacles continue to frustrate efforts to improve vessel arrivals and reduce unnecessary waiting outside ports. Despite years of work on just-in-time arrivals, ships continue to waste fuel at anchor because the interests of owners, charterers and terminal operators rarely line up. “It comes down to who pays and who benefits,” Simha explains. Slowing a ship can save its owner fuel, but charterparty arrangements may favour faster steaming, while terminals operate under different commercial pressures. The cost of this disconnect is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. Citing VesselBot data, Simha points out that Mediterranean port calls spent more than ten hours on average at anchor during the final quarter of 2025, roughly twice the waiting time recorded in China and East Asia and around a third higher than a year earlier. He believes meaningful improvements will require common definitions of arrival and readiness, alongside contracts that distribute the financial benefits of more efficient operations. Rather than trying to change the entire industry at once, he favours starting with one port and a small group of shipping and terminal partners willing to put the model into practice. Looking back on his years at MSC and the industry’s wider digital transformation, Simha identifies a more fundamental problem that has persisted through successive generations of technology. “We digitalised paper, not the process,” he observes. “For decades each company built its own version of the same thing, with its own definitions and its own formats.” The result has been years of work connecting systems that were never designed to communicate with one another. By 2035, Simha wants ships, ports, terminals, rail operators and trucking companies working from a common set of trusted information, allowing delays and changes in vessel schedules to be communicated across the supply chain as they happen. “If a vessel is delayed, everyone in the chain knows at the same time, and everyone adjusts,” he says. Getting there will require more than new software or another round of technology investment. For Simha, changing how people and companies work together remains just as important as the systems they use. “Resistance to change is natural. We resisted the telex and email, and later couldn’t imagine life without them.” Tags Switzerland Splash November 18, 2026 0 273 4 minutes read Follow Us Facebook X LinkedIn Tumblr Pinterest Reddit VKontakte Messenger Messenger WhatsApp Telegram Share via Email Print

The proposed facility aims to improve container movements between Cambodia’s industrial and commercial centres and international shipping networks, particularly through the Port of Sihanoukville. The agreement outlines plans to combine rail, road and maritime transport within an integrated logistics platform. The project remains at the planning and feasibility stage, with no construction timetable announced. Proposed hub to include container and rail facilities The planned development would include a dry port, container-handling yard, empty container depot and container freight station (CFS). It would also provide rail-connected container-handling facilities, allowing cargo to move between inland logistics operations and the Port of Sihanoukville. Under the proposed cooperation, Royal Railway will be responsible for providing and maintaining rail access and connectivity. The company will also support related railway infrastructure and road access. Meanwhile, CMA CGM Inland Services (CCIS) will lead the operational concept, commercial feasibility assessment and business plan. CCIS will also coordinate design, technical and environmental studies, alongside the proposed phases of development. “Through this proposed platform in Phnom Penh, we see an opportunity to strengthen connectivity between inland logistics and maritime transport, particularly through the Port of Sihanoukville, while supporting the evolving needs of our customers and Cambodia’s growing trade flows,” said Kaushal Rohilla, General Manager, CMA CGM Cambodia. Rohilla also highlighted the importance of cooperation with Sihanoukville Autonomous Port and Royal Railway in assessing the project’s potential. Strengthening Cambodia’s intermodal connections The proposed logistics platform would build on Cambodia’s existing railway network, which already supports container movements between Phnom Penh and Sihanoukville. The initiative aims to provide additional options for cargo handling, storage and inland distribution, particularly for businesses moving containers through the country’s main maritime gateway. Royal Railway will work with CMA CGM Inland Services to develop the operating and commercial arrangements for the proposed rail services. Neak Oknha Kith Meng, Chairman of Royal Group of Companies, said the cooperation aims to improve connections between different modes of transport and support Cambodia’s long-term trade development. The agreement represents an initial step towards a more integrated logistics network linking Cambodia’s inland markets with international container shipping services. The companies have not disclosed an investment value, expected handling capacity or target completion date for the proposed platform.

articles.title: How the Hormuz crisis handed America a lasting export advantage
articles.summary: As Middle Eastern supplies faltered, American exporters of LNG, LPG, jet fuel and plastics gained new customers, new shipping routes and, in some cases, contracts stretching decades into the future. Alex Byelyavtsev reports. When the Strait of Hormuz became unreliable in 2026, some of the world’s largest suppliers of...
articles.body: Americas Containers Contributions Dry Cargo Gas Middle East Tankers How the Hormuz crisis handed America a lasting export advantage Splash November 18, 2026 0 1,430 3 minutes read Caturus Caturus As Middle Eastern supplies faltered, American exporters of LNG, LPG, jet fuel and plastics gained new customers, new shipping routes and, in some cases, contracts stretching decades into the future. Alex Byelyavtsev reports. When the Strait of Hormuz became unreliable in 2026, some of the world’s largest suppliers of energy and industrial materials lost their normal access to customers overseas. The customers did not disappear. Power stations still needed gas. Airlines needed fuel. Factories needed raw materials. So buyers looked elsewhere. And for several important products, the search led to the same place: the United States. American producers found new customers, export terminals handled additional cargo, and shipping companies faced different voyages. Consider natural gas. Qatar is one of the world’s largest exporters. In October, its national energy company agreed to buy American gas under contracts lasting decades. The reason was straightforward. If Qatar cannot export its own gas through Hormuz, it can still trade cargo loaded elsewhere and earn revenue from markets it would otherwise struggle to serve. American exporter Cheniere has secured agreements to supply QatarEnergy with 4m tonnes of gas annually through 2054. The gas is sold at the American loading terminal. QatarEnergy arranges the vessel and decides where to deliver it. Deliveries are due to begin in the early 2030s. Part of the volume still depends on an investment decision. What began as a search for alternative supply is becoming a long-term commercial commitment. The wider shift in LNG trade was already visible in 2026. American LNG shipments to Asia rose 108% in the first half of 2026. The disruption contributed to that increase, although new US production capacity was also coming online. Finding another supplier did not mean finding a shorter route. Of 34 American LNG cargoes heading to Asia-Pacific in April, 31 sailed around the Cape of Good Hope rather than through the Panama Canal. The alternative supply was available, but the voyage was not the same. But gas was only one part of the shift. American propane exports reached a record 2.1m barrels a day in April as Asian buyers sought alternatives to disrupted Middle Eastern supplies. Enterprise Products Partners was already expanding propane and butane export capacity at its Houston Ship Channel terminal by another 300,000 barrels a day, illustrating how established American terminals were positioned to handle greater demand. The shipping calculation changed with the cargo. A buyer who previously received propane from the Persian Gulf might now need a gas carrier to collect it in Texas. That can mean a longer voyage, additional fuel and a different choice of route. For cargo heading to East Asia, the Panama Canal may shorten the passage, but access is not always immediate or inexpensive. Going around takes more time. Either way, a vessel occupied for longer cannot carry its next cargo as soon. For the buyer, the alternative supply exists. For the shipowner, the extra sailing days may create additional employment. For the cargo owner, those same days can become an additional cost. Something similar happened with aviation fuel. As supplies from the Middle East tightened, American refineries increased production for export. According to US government energy data, jet-fuel exports averaged 356,000 barrels a day in the second quarter of 2026, more than double the five-year average. Some refineries adjusted production to meet overseas demand. Product tankers carried additional cargo across the Atlantic. Container shipping tells a slightly different story. The American Gulf Coast was already an important supplier of plastic materials used by manufacturers worldwide. Plastics and resins accounted for about 45% of Port Houston’s containerised export teu in 2025. The infrastructure was there when overseas buyers began looking for replacement supplies. When Middle Eastern supplies became harder to obtain, American producers received more orders and container bookings increased. Across the United States, exporters booked more than 6,000 containers of plastic materials in a single day in March, well above normal levels. Those exports could fill space on return voyages that might otherwise have sailed lighter. The surge later eased. The gas contracts were different. Those commitments extend for decades. Put these markets together and a pattern emerges. Natural gas, propane, refined products and plastics travel on different ships and through different terminals. Their markets are not interchangeable. But several of them found American producers, American terminals and American load ports when the usual suppliers could not deliver. That does not make the United States the only beneficiary or the only alternative supplier. A company may replace a disrupted Middle Eastern source with an American one. Its contract is secure, the cargo is available, and a ship can be arranged. The disruption opened markets that American producers did not previously serve on the same terms. Some orders were temporary. Others became long-term commitments, bringing new loading ports, shipping routes and commercial relationships. The question is not simply where the cargo moved during the crisis. It is how much of that business will move back when the original suppliers return. articles.title: DP World reports 50,000 tonnes of avoided emissions through Southampton rail scheme

articles.body: DP World says its Modal Shift Programme at Southampton has helped avoid an estimated 50,000 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent emissions since its launch in 2023, as more imported containers move inland by rail rather than road. According to the company, the programme has supported the movement of more than 220,000 additional containers by rail, avoiding an estimated 18 million miles of road transport over the past three years. The initiative uses financial incentives to encourage cargo owners to choose rail for inland container movements from DP World Southampton. The company reported that rail’s share of container movements at the port increased from 21% when the programme began to 29% in its latest update. DP World also attributed the introduction of five rail services linking Southampton with Birmingham, Cardiff, East Midlands Gateway, Doncaster and Northampton partly to the programme. Rail incentives support inland container movements Launched in September 2023, the Modal Shift Programme was designed to make rail transport more commercially attractive for import-laden containers. The scheme provides incentives for qualifying containers moved by rail to destinations within a designated zone extending approximately 140 miles from Southampton. It is funded through a £10 fee applied to all import-laden containers arriving at the port. “Decarbonising supply chains requires practical solutions that make commercial sense for customers,” said Kris Adams, CEO, UK Ports and Terminals, DP World. “Our Modal Shift Programme shows what can be achieved when we work with our partners to make lower-emission transport options more accessible and attractive,” Adams added. The programme has undergone several adjustments since its introduction, including changes to the incentives available to customers and rail freight operators. Its existing framework also provides performance-based payments to eligible Rail Freight Terminal Operators (RFTOs), subject to meeting volume targets. Under the arrangements applying during the final quarter of 2026, qualifying operators can receive incentives linked to the number of import-laden containers transported by rail within the programme’s designated zone. The latest performance figures mark another milestone for the Southampton initiative, which had already supported the movement of 100,000 additional containers by rail by March 2025. DP World said it intends to explore further opportunities to expand the programme across its UK operations. The company has not announced additional locations or implementation dates for any future expansion.

articles.body: Aalborg Container Terminal in Denmark is joining the Portchain Connect network to improve berth planning and communication with shipping lines. The terminal will use the digital platform to exchange vessel schedules and operational information directly with carriers. The system will also allow both sides to coordinate berthing windows through a shared digital process. Through Portchain Connect, Aalborg Container Terminal will receive real-time updates on vessel schedules and container move counts. Terminal planners will then be able to respond to changes and propose alternative berthing arrangements. The implementation aims to improve coordination between vessel arrivals and terminal operations while reducing manual communication. Digital coordination supports feeder operations Aalborg Container Terminal serves northern Denmark through weekly feeder connections with Hamburg and Bremerhaven, linking regional cargo flows to international container shipping networks. The terminal also provides direct road and rail access, supporting multimodal freight movements. The new system is intended to improve the exchange of operational data between the terminal and its shipping line customers. Earlier access to schedule updates should help planners adjust berth availability and coordinate vessel calls more efficiently. “We’re pleased to welcome Aalborg Container Terminal to the Portchain Network. As an important gateway connecting Northern Denmark to global container trade, earlier alignment between terminals and carriers supports more predictable and efficient vessel planning,” said Thor Thorup, CCO and Co-Founder, Portchain. According to Portchain, its network connects more than 200 container terminals and six major container carriers, representing over 40% of global terminal capacity. The platform supports digital agreements on berthing windows and provides access to live vessel tracking and terminal lineup information. The Aalborg agreement follows the recent adoption of Portchain Connect by Euroports’ container terminal in Rauma, Finland, as the software provider continues expanding its network across European ports. Portchain did not disclose the financial terms of the Aalborg agreement or a timetable for completing the implementation.

articles.body: DHL Supply Chain expects the total value of new customer contracts signed during 2026 to exceed €8 billion, as businesses increase demand for long-term logistics partnerships. The contract logistics division of DHL Group also reported a qualified commercial pipeline of more than €36 billion. The company attributed this demand to changing trade patterns, geopolitical uncertainty and the need for more resilient supply chains. The projected €8 billion figure represents Total Contract Value (TCV), which measures the lifetime value of customer agreements rather than annual revenue. According to DHL Supply Chain, the expected contract value is spread across several regions and industries. The Americas are projected to account for approximately 45% of the total, followed by Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA) at 35% and Asia Pacific at 20%. Revenue growth supports expansion DHL Supply Chain also reported a 12% increase in third-quarter revenue compared with the same period in 2025. Growth was recorded across all major regions. Revenue increased by 13.1% in the Americas, 11.7% in EMEA and 9.9% in Asia Pacific. The company said demand remained strong across several industries, including healthcare, technology, retail, automotive and new energy. “Supply chain resilience has become a strategic differentiator for many companies,” said Hendrik Venter, CEO, DHL Supply Chain. Venter added that customers increasingly require logistics partners capable of managing complex operations while improving flexibility and productivity. The company operates in more than 55 countries and reports a contract renewal rate of approximately 90%. DHL expands logistics capabilities and automation To support future growth, DHL Supply Chain is investing in artificial intelligence, robotics and warehouse automation. It is also expanding specialised logistics services in selected industries. In healthcare, the company has strengthened its relationship with pharmaceutical manufacturer Sanofi. After managing three distribution sites since 2024, DHL took over operations at Sanofi’s vaccine distribution centre in Val-de-Reuil, France, in 2026. DHL is also developing additional pharmaceutical warehousing capacity. Its global network currently includes more than 250 pharmaceutical warehouses. Meanwhile, the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure and data centres is creating further demand for specialised logistics services. DHL Supply Chain is targeting opportunities across the data centre industry, including the transportation and handling of sensitive equipment. The company is also developing capabilities for battery logistics and other emerging industries. These investments support DHL Supply Chain’s strategy of expanding its customer relationships and increasing operational efficiency. Looking ahead, the company aims to grow at least two percentage points faster than each contract logistics market in which it operates. The growth strategy combines long-term customer agreements with investments in technology, infrastructure and specialised supply chain services.

articles.title: ITF joins ISF Verify initiative to expand digital seafarer certification
articles.summary: The International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF) has joined the ISF Verify initiative, supporting efforts to expand digital seafarer certification across the global shipping industry. The agreement was signed during Hong Kong Maritime Week on 17 November 2026, bringing the ITF into a project developed by the...
articles.body: The International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF) has joined the ISF Verify initiative, supporting efforts to expand digital seafarer certification across the global shipping industry. The agreement was signed during Hong Kong Maritime Week on 17 November 2026, bringing the ITF into a project developed by the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) and Lloyd’s Register OneOcean. Through the cooperation, the initiative will gain access to the ITF’s seafarer network, which reaches approximately one million seafarers across more than 100 countries. The ITF and its inspectorate will also provide feedback to help ensure that the platform meets the practical needs of seafarers. Expanding access to digital certification ISF Verify is a cloud-based platform designed to replace paper-based certification processes with secure digital verification. The system connects seafarers, maritime administrations, port state control authorities and shipping companies, allowing certificates to be shared, checked and endorsed electronically. A key feature is that seafarers retain control over access to their personal information. They can decide who can view their certificate data and withdraw permission when necessary. The platform also operates as a connector between existing certification systems rather than a central database. Original certificate records remain with the issuing maritime authorities. The initiative aims to reduce administrative requirements while improving the efficiency of certificate verification across international shipping. “Digitalisation must work for seafarers – and that means ensuring that seafarers’ voices are heard so that we know that this technology will make their working lives easier through straightforward, secure and accessible certification,” said Stephen Cotton, General Secretary, International Transport Workers’ Federation. Cotton highlighted the role of ITF inspectors in gathering feedback from seafarers during the platform’s development. Initiative builds on progress in India and the Philippines The latest agreement follows the participation of India’s Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA) earlier in November. India joined the initiative to explore connecting its national certification system with ISF Verify through a technical integration programme. The project has also completed a proof of concept with the Philippines’ Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA), creating a foundation for further implementation. Together, India and the Philippines represent approximately 30% of the global seafarer workforce, according to the ICS. However, their participation does not mean that all seafarers in those countries are already using the platform. “The industry needs a single, trusted connector that respects national jurisdiction authority while removing needless paper burden,” said Thomas A. Kazakos, Secretary General, International Chamber of Shipping. The ITF’s involvement is expected to provide additional input as the project moves towards wider international adoption. Under the initiative’s proposed operating model, seafarers will continue to have free access to their certificates through the mobile application. The partners have not announced a timetable for completing the global rollout.

U.S. Coast Guard Photo The U.S. Coast Guard’s newest polar icebreaker, Storis (WAGB 21), has returned to Seattle following a 133-day Arctic deployment that included monitoring Chinese research vessels, conducting fisheries enforcement operations and testing military capabilities in ice-covered waters. The 360-foot cutter returned to its temporary homeport on Saturday, November 14, after traveling more than 17,000 nautical miles through the Arctic Ocean and waters around Alaska. According to the Coast Guard, Storis served as the sole U.S. surface asset in the High Arctic during portions of its deployment, supporting maritime security, border enforcement and sovereignty missions. Under Operation Frontier Sentinel, the cutter spent more than 300 hours monitoring foreign-flagged research vessels, including four Chinese-flagged ships operating over the U.S. extended continental shelf. The patrol also marked the first designated law enforcement mission conducted by a U.S. polar icebreaker in more than 20 years. The crew inspected fishing vessels in the Bering Sea, including a joint boarding and fisheries processing plant inspection with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Office of Law Enforcement. In another milestone, Storis conducted what the Coast Guard described as the first live-fire gunnery exercise by one of its surface vessels operating in ice-covered Arctic waters in decades. The exercise was intended to assess weapons employment in extreme conditions and generate data to guide future Arctic operations. The cutter also conducted a simulated replenishment-at-sea exercise with Coast Guard Cutter Stratton near Unalaska, Alaska. Crews used Storis’ dynamic positioning system and onboard sensors to demonstrate close-quarters maneuvering capabilities needed for replenishment operations in remote waters. During Operation Tundra Merlin, Storis operated alongside Coast Guard cutters Munro and Fir and the Royal Canadian Navy’s HMCS Max Bernays, strengthening coordination between U.S. and Canadian forces. The cutter also assisted the grounded fishing vessel Aleutian Dream, providing initial assistance and escorting the vessel back to Dutch Harbor. “We are serving in a moment of great change in our service, nation and world,” said Capt. Corey Kerns, commanding officer of Storis. He said the crew’s efforts had transformed the vessel into an operational, multi-mission military asset. The deployment included testing unmanned aircraft in extreme cold alongside the Coast Guard Research and Development Center and the Defense Innovation Unit. Five sorties totaling nine flight hours evaluated drone performance in high-latitude conditions, supporting the Icebreaker Collaboration Effort between the United States, Canada and Finland. Storis, formerly the commercial icebreaking vessel Aiviq, was acquired by the Coast Guard in December 2024 and commissioned in August 2025, becoming the service’s first new polar icebreaker in more than two decades. The deployment comes as the Coast Guard’s already limited polar icebreaking fleet faces continued strain. The service’s medium icebreaker Healy has been sidelined since suffering a major engineering casualty in July, forcing the cancellation of its planned 2026 Arctic mission. The situation underscores Washington’s continuing struggle to maintain polar capabilities as competition with Russia and China intensifies. REUTERS/Stringer/File Photo By Arsalan Shahla and Jen Judson (Bloomberg) — American warplanes hit an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Persian Gulf on Tuesday, a US military official said, as the two sides intensified tit-for-tat attacks in the ongoing war. The strike on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps site was in response to Iranian aggression targeting US personnel and assets, the official said, declining to be named. Earlier on Tuesday, Iran’s semi-official Mehr News Agency reported that US forces had struck several locations on Qeshm Island, adding the assault caused no casualties or damage to critical and public-service infrastructure. The US bombing came after the third Iranian attack on Bahrain in less than a week. President Donald Trump separately said the US is investigating a report about potential Iranian plans to target Washington. The flurry of recent incidents — as well as increased Iranian attacks on commercial vessels — suggests an intensification of the low-grade clashes that have persisted throughout the ongoing stalemate between the US and Iran. “For both the US and Iran, there’s an operational rationale for their strikes, from reducing threats to their ability to operate in the Strait of Hormuz,” said Becca Wasser, defense lead for Bloomberg Economics. “But we’ve seen throughout this conflict the mismatch between operational objectives and political realities, where tit-for-tat strikes quickly escalate.” Neither side has shown a willingness to compromise on an issue that might pave the way to a resolution, such as the lifting of a US naval blockade or concessions from Iran on its nuclear program. Qatar, the main mediator between Washington and Tehran, was due to meet with representatives of the Islamic Republic on Tuesday, part of a long-running effort to find a diplomatic off-ramp. Oil prices gained amid the fresh flareups, having plunged following the Republican defeat in the US midterm elections earlier this month. Brent crude rose toward $94 a barrel, still up more than 50% for the year. Qeshm lies off Iran’s southern coast near the Strait of Hormuz — the critical transit point for oil and gas that’s long been the focal point of the conflict. The US launched limited attacks on the island earlier this month, saying they were defensive in nature and designed to help energy tankers and other vessels get through the strait safely. Earlier Tuesday, Iran’s parliamentary speaker and lead negotiator with the US, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, warned that Tehran would retaliate against civilian infrastructure near US and Israeli bases if Washington did the same. His comments, a standard Iranian response to any perceived indication of US escalation, followed a New York Times report that water infrastructure sites in Iran “may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup.” This amounted to “prepping the next round on civilian” infrastructure, Ghalibaf said. “We’ll apply your logic consistently and even-handedly.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: Vestas CEO Calls For EU Crackdown on Chinese Software Used in Wind Sector
articles.summary: As the European Union weighs tougher cybersecurity rules, it should consider a ban on Chinese components and technology containing software in critical energy infrastructure, the CEO of Danish wind turbine maker Vestas told Reuters."When it comes to critical infrastructure…
articles.body: Vestas CEO Calls For EU Crackdown on Chinese Software Used in Wind Sector Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 17, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Peter Adams As the European Union weighs tougher cybersecurity rules, it should consider a ban on Chinese components and technology containing software in critical energy infrastructure, the CEO of Danish wind turbine maker Vestas told Reuters. "When it comes to critical infrastructure, meaning technology or components that has a software element in it, I think we should have a very upfront 'no thank you'," CEO Henrik Andersen said when asked whether Europe should adopt rules similar to China’s restrictions on foreign technology. "The energy assets you build now last 30 to 50 years, and you have to make sure you can control them yourself," he said. The European Union is revising its cybersecurity rules and requirements for European-made equipment while governments expand their power grids to handle increased renewable energy supply. China's commerce ministry has said it would take strong countermeasures if the bloc adopts the revised Cybersecurity Act proposed in January, arguing the law would abandon technological neutrality and undermine China-EU trade. Chinese manufacturers supplied a fraction of Europe's new turbines last year but are pushing to enter the market. Vestas' Andersen said the EU should require that about half of its wind assets are made in Europe, and that a turbine’s control systems and software should be treated separately from that requirement. A German developer dropped China's Ming Yang from a North Sea project last year. Britain said in March it would not support the use of turbines from China's Ming Yang in UK offshore wind on security grounds. Ming Yang in a statement to Reuters on Monday said it stores all turbine data locally in Europe, that operators retain full control, and that no remote access is permitted without the operator's explicit approval. CHINA HAS ALSO TIGHTENED RULES Andersen noted that Chinese authorities have imposed similar rules, telling Vestas that it could no longer monitor the sensors on its own turbines or update its turbines' software remotely from Europe, on the grounds that foreign access posed a risk to China's grid. "China put a marker in the sand five years ago, and now it's time that we say that marker counts on both sides," Andersen told Reuters at the company's headquarters in Copenhagen. Chinese utilities are replacing Western equipment with domestic alternatives, Poland's state-funded Centre for Eastern Studies said in a report last month. Andersen, whose company stands to gain if Chinese rivals are kept out of Europe, said he did not support a blanket ban on Chinese components but that if Europe believed in free competition, Vestas should have the same access to China's market, which it no longer has. "If we are going to play football, then let's play football. Eleven a side and a referee in the middle," he said. He said attacks that cranked up fridge temperatures at supermarkets across Europe this month were a reminder that whoever holds the software updates controls the machine, whether it is a refrigerator, car or wind turbine. While no one has claimed responsibility for those attacks, they have heightened concerns among European authorities about hybrid threats to infrastructure. "There is a security risk if you are not the one holding the username, password and access," Andersen said. Ming Yang in the written statement said it also supported cybersecurity rules being applied equally to every supplier, but added that supplier-specific assessment and verifiable safeguards were preferable to "blanket exclusions based on country of origin". The China Chamber of Commerce to the EU and China’s commerce ministry did not respond to requests for comment. (Reuters)

articles.summary: The number of empty tankers sailing to collect cargoes of Middle East crude is sliding, a trend that could jeopardize the recent revival in the region’s oil flows to global markets, according to Tankertrackers.com, a firm that monitors vessel movements.

Join the leading maritime news network Stock Photo: Faraways/Shutterstock By Alaric Nightingale (Bloomberg) — The number of empty tankers sailing to collect cargoes of Middle East crude is sliding, a trend that could jeopardize the recent revival in the region’s oil flows to global markets, according to Tankertrackers.com, a firm that monitors vessel movements. The industry uses two main ship types to get oil from the Persian Gulf to the world: very large crude carriers, which transport 2 million-barrel cargoes, and Suezmaxes that move about half that. The collective capacity of those vessels sailing empty to the region has declined by about 40% since the end of August, according to Tankertrackers.com figures. While the market is intensely focused on how much oil leaves the Middle East, those flows are only possible if there’s a steady stream of ships arriving to pick up the barrels. The Iran war has meant that some vessels refuse to go through the Strait of Hormuz, instead receiving cargoes in locations like the Gulf of Oman from tankers that are willing to risk shuttling through the crucial waterway. There are “not enough vacant tankers to take oil out of the region,” Tankertrackers.com’s co-founder, Samir Madani, said by WhatsApp. “It’s one thing to bring the oil out into the Gulf of Oman via the Strait of Hormuz, but it seems like there isn’t enough to take the oil out of the Gulf of Oman.” In broad terms, there has been a dip in flows from the region at large so far this month, though it’s still unclear what the causes of the drop are, the exact scale of the decrease, or how long-lasting the decline will be, Madani said. For now, though, the number of ships transferring cargoes onto other ships outside the Persian Gulf remains high, enabling shipments toward customers to continue for the time being, he said. Oil tanker rates have declined from record levels over the past few weeks, helping to reduce the cost of delivering crude to customers. Any shortage in the number of empty vessels would support rates. Iran has attacked shipping consistently throughout the conflict, something that has deterred transits. The number of incidents reported officially jumped last month, and remains at high levels so far in November, according to data from the International Maritime Organization and the UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P.
