articles.title: NTSB Warned of Mississippi River Passenger Vessel Collision Risks Nearly 30 Years Ago
articles.summary: Nearly three decades before a tanker slammed into a docked river cruise ship in New Orleans, the National Transportation Safety Board warned that passenger vessels along the Mississippi River waterfront...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network The bulk carrier Bright Field surrounded by tugboats near the damaged New Orleans waterfront following its December 1996 allision. The accident prompted NTSB safety recommendations addressing the risks posed by large commercial vessels to passenger ships docked along the Mississippi River. (Image: NTSB accident investigation report) Nearly three decades before a tanker slammed into a docked river cruise ship in New Orleans, the National Transportation Safety Board warned that passenger vessels along the Mississippi River waterfront were vulnerable to being struck by large commercial ships and urged authorities to consider relocating them or installing protective measures. The warning came in a 1998 NTSB investigation into the Bright Field accident, when a Liberian-flagged bulk carrier lost propulsion and crashed into the New Orleans riverfront, injuring 62 people. Now, the findings are drawing renewed attention following Friday’s allision between the Marshall Islands-flagged tanker Atlantic Asphalt and American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage , which capsized after being struck while docked near the Crescent City Connection Bridge right in the heart of downtown New Orleans. All 190 passengers and crew aboard the riverboat survived the November 13 accident, although 32 people were taken to hospitals. The similarities between the two accidents are striking, particularly because the earlier investigation specifically identified the dangers facing passenger vessels moored along the busy commercial waterway. In its report on the December 14, 1996, Bright Field accident, the NTSB concluded that the Coast Guard, Port of New Orleans and waterfront operators had failed to adequately assess, manage or mitigate the risks of locating unprotected commercial facilities in areas vulnerable to vessel strikes. Notably, the Bright Field stopped just 70 feet from the docked gaming vessel Queen of New Orleans , while its bow wave caused the gangway of the nearby paddlewheeler Creole Queen to collapse, sending three passengers into the Mississippi River. The Creole Queen had 190 passengers and crew aboard — the same approximate number reported aboard American Heritage during Friday’s collision. The NTSB subsequently criticized the vessels’ emergency evacuation arrangements and issued additional safety recommendations. In its report, the agency issued two recommendations addressing the placement of passenger vessels along the river. Recommendation M-98-1 directed the Coast Guard, working with the Port of New Orleans, to reassess the risks of passenger vessel berths along the Mississippi River’s left descending bank and determine whether vessels should be moved to safer locations or protected through procedural, operational or physical barriers. Another recommendation, M-98-10, directed the Port of New Orleans to undertake the same assessment in cooperation with the Coast Guard. The NTSB also called for a comprehensive risk assessment of maritime and shoreside activities throughout the port, including measures to reduce the dangers associated with commercial vessel traffic. In that earlier investigation, the NTSB highlighted the risks created by large vessels navigating the narrow, heavily trafficked river near passenger terminals, commercial developments and other vulnerable infrastructure, and identified potential mitigation measures including reduced vessel speeds, tug escorts and moving passenger vessels to safer locations. The danger of mechanical failure was also well documented. When the Coast Guard subsequently finalized additional Lower Mississippi River navigation regulations in 1999, it noted that more than 300 self-propelled vessels of at least 1,600 gross tons had experienced propulsion losses, steering casualties or engine irregularities on the Mississippi River during 1995 and 1996. The 1999 regulations established additional operating requirements for larger commercial vessels and required certain passenger vessels moored or anchored in the river to maintain manned pilothouse watches and monitor emergency communications. Those requirements, now contained in 33 CFR 165.810 , were intended to improve navigation safety and allow passenger vessel crews to respond quickly to emergencies. The regulatory action demonstrates that authorities did respond to the earlier accident. However, the extent to which the NTSB’s separate recommendations concerning passenger vessel placement and protective barriers were implemented at individual berths remains unclear. The current official disposition of recommendations M-98-1 and M-98-10 has not been independently confirmed. Nor has it been established what specific risk assessments or protective measures were in place at the berth occupied by American Heritage . Those questions could become significant as investigators examine the circumstances surrounding Friday’s collision. According to the NTSB’s ongoing investigation , the Atlantic Asphalt was traveling upriver near the Crescent City Connection Bridge when it experienced what investigators described as a steering casualty. Preliminary information recovered from the tanker’s voyage data recorder indicates the vessel’s rudder remained in a starboard position, causing the tanker to veer toward the river’s east bank. Approximately two minutes later, the tanker struck American Heritage at its berth. The riverboat subsequently overturned, forcing passengers and crew to evacuate as emergency responders and nearby commercial vessels rushed to assist. Investigators have not determined what caused the steering failure. While the Bright Field accident involved a loss of propulsion rather than steering, both incidents demonstrate the consequences of a large commercial vessel losing maneuvering capability in the confined waters of downtown New Orleans. The NTSB has not determined whether the location of the American Heritage berth or the protective measures in place contributed to Friday’s accident. Nor is there evidence at this stage that either vessel or port authorities violated the regulations adopted following the earlier casualty. But the 1998 recommendations raise an important question nearly 30 years after federal investigators identified the danger of large commercial ships striking passenger vessels along the New Orleans waterfront. For the NTSB, which has repeatedly warned across transportation sectors about the dangers of leaving identified safety risks unresolved, the latest collision presents another opportunity to examine whether lessons from an earlier accident could have made a difference in this latest case. articles.title: US Military Radar System in Bahrain Attacked by Iran
articles.summary: Iran fired drones at a US military radar system in Bahrain on Tuesday and the crew of a tanker was reported missing in the Strait of Hormuz, despite talks between Iran and mediators Oman and Qatar.Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said…
articles.body: US Military Radar System in Bahrain Attacked by Iran Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 17, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Zerophoto Iran fired drones at a US military radar system in Bahrain on Tuesday and the crew of a tanker was reported missing in the Strait of Hormuz, despite talks between Iran and mediators Oman and Qatar. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said the radar system at Bahrain's Sheikh Isa base had been targeted, and warned Bahrain over its alliance with the US and stance towards Shi'ite clergy. Bahrain, which is home to the headquarters of the US Fifth Fleet, said it had intercepted the attack and there were no reports of casualties or damage. Later on Tuesday, Iranian media reported an explosion on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, and cited an Iranian official as saying the US had carried out an attack there without causing damage to infrastructure. Asked for comment, the US military's Central Command said it had no updates. Washington carried out limited strikes on Qeshm earlier this month. Qatari and Iranian officials were meeting on Tuesday, Qatar said, as part of efforts to mediate an end to nearly nine months of war that has destabilised the Middle East and pushed up global energy prices. The talks are aimed at "bridging perspectives and narrowing the gap between proposals presented on the ground," Qatari spokesperson Majed Al Ansari said. They coincide with a visit to Oman by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi. Oman's Foreign Ministry said he discussed safeguarding maritime corridors and ensuring the smooth flow of global shipping and trade, as well as preventing military escalation, with Oman's foreign minister. Oman and Iran lie on opposite sides of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway that carried about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies before the war but is now partly blocked by Iran. Oman has previously held talks with Tehran about controlling traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Araqchi said in a post on Telegram that he also met Oman's Sultan Haitham ‌bin Tariq and informed him about Iran's diplomatic initiative to end the war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28. RISE IN ATTACKS ON TANKERS The war has ground to a stalemate, with US President Donald Trump saying he might hold off from attacking Iran if the US does not face what he described as provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthi group in Yemen. Trump said on Tuesday the US was taking seriously the possibility that Iran could be ‌planning an attack involving a so-called dirty bomb in Washington, after being asked about a CNN report citing US intelligence assessments. Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson said the report was part of a US campaign "to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs" using "baseless allegations". Trump has also said he will maintain a US naval blockade on Iran because it has continued to disrupt shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, which is a sticking point in negotiations. Attacks on tankers have increased this month in the strait, and the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said the crew of a tanker passing through the waterway was unaccounted for after being attacked north of ⁠the Omani port city of Khasab. Iran's Revolutionary Guards and navy said on Tuesday that a ship carrying LNG and two oil tankers had caught fire in the strait. Reuters could not independently verify the reports. Benchmark Brent crude futures were up 0.4% at $92.76 a barrel on Tuesday, much higher than before the war but well below April's wartime peak of $126.41. IRANIAN WARNING The war also continues to spill over into other parts of the Middle East as Iran puts pressure on Washington through its Houthi allies, who have carried out attacks on Saudi Arabia and seized areas along the Yemeni coast on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, hoping to squeeze Gulf oil producers. Tuesday's attack on Bahrain, a Shi'ite-majority country ruled by a Sunni Muslim family, followed the sentencing there of 64 people, mostly Shi'ite clerics, to life in prison on charges of colluding with Iran to undermine the state. Iran's foreign ministry condemned the court's ruling on Tuesday and said the accusations were baseless. Tehran has long denied interference in Bahrain's internal affairs. Iran also fired on Bahrain two days ago,saying it had targeted a US radar system at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base following what it said were hostile US actions. Iran's Revolutionary Guards spokesperson said Bahrain had made "three key mistakes", which he listed as "cooperating in the invasion of the Islamic Republic of Iran, remaining within the US security bubble, and encroaching on the sanctity of Shi'ite religious authority". These, "if continued, will jeopardize its survival in the region's new security order," ⁠Hossein Mohebbi said. (Reuters)

articles.summary: Norway is moving a step closer to testing nuclear propulsion for commercial ships, with a consortium including shipbuilder VARD and offshore vessel operator Island Offshore securing NOK 20 million ($2...

VARD/Island Offshore Norway is moving a step closer to testing nuclear propulsion for commercial ships, with a consortium including shipbuilder VARD and offshore vessel operator Island Offshore securing NOK 20 million ($2 million) in government funding to develop an integrated nuclear power system for offshore vessels. The Marine Nuclear Propulsion System (MarNuPS) project , led by Emerald Nuclear Norway, aims to move the technology from engineering studies into full-scale testing, with a first vessel deployment targeted for 2031 or 2032. The initial funding comes from the Research Council of Norway and supports a broader development program that will bring together reactor technology, ship design, electrical systems and vessel operations. The first phase, scheduled for 2027, will establish a test facility at Stette, near Ålesund, where the partners plan to assemble and test a full-scale representation of the proposed shipboard propulsion system. Importantly, the initial testing will not involve an operating nuclear reactor. Instead, the system will use electric heating to simulate the reactor’s thermal output, allowing engineers to evaluate how the propulsion and power systems work together before moving to nuclear operation. Testing will examine normal vessel operations, rapid changes in power demand, system performance, stress conditions and crew interaction. The project is based on Emerald Nuclear’s 5-megawatt-electric GEM Microreactor technology, using a gas-cooled reactor design coupled with a supercritical carbon dioxide turbine system to generate electricity. The integrated system will also include energy storage, remote monitoring, power management and shipboard automation. According to Emerald Nuclear , the first phase has an estimated total cost of NOK 150 million ($15.6 million), with project partners providing substantial funding beyond the government grant. For VARD, part of Italy’s Fincantieri Group, the project represents another step toward bringing advanced nuclear technology into commercial shipbuilding. Its subsidiary Vard Electro will focus on integrating the power system with the electrical controls and automation systems used aboard ships. “We also view this funding award as a vital sign of national support for nuclear applications in maritime going forward,” said Håvard Vollset Lien, Vice President of Research and Innovation at Vard Group. Island Offshore, meanwhile, hopes to become the first offshore service vessel operator to install the system. “Nuclear energy has the potential to provide a new route to decarbonising offshore vessels without compromising the power, endurance and operational flexibility these ships require,” said Tommy Walaunet, CEO of Island Offshore. Emerald Nuclear is also proposing a different commercial model for shipboard nuclear power. Rather than requiring shipowners to purchase and operate reactors themselves, the company would retain ownership and operational responsibility, including maintenance and nuclear fuel management. Shipowners would instead pay for the electricity they use. The consortium also includes the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Imperial College London and engineering specialist Maskindynamikk, bringing together expertise in nuclear modelling, structural integrity, monitoring and marine operations. The project builds on Norway’s earlier NuProShip research initiatives, which have examined the feasibility of nuclear propulsion for commercial shipping. While significant technical testing, safety validation and regulatory work remain before the technology can be deployed at sea, the next phase will provide an early full-scale demonstration of how a nuclear energy system could be integrated into an offshore vessel. (Photo: Hanwha Defense USA) South Korea’s Hanwha Aerospace and its U.S. subsidiary have successfully test-fired a Chunmoo guided missile from a vessel off the Mississippi coast, marking another step toward deploying precision-strike weapons aboard crewed and unmanned naval vessels. The launch took place Sunday, November 15, aboard a test-range vessel operated by Mississippi-based The Spaceport Company , using a palletized launcher designed to be installed on maritime platforms. According to Hanwha Defense USA, the firing completed a two-launch test campaign aimed at validating the Chunmoo missile system for operations at sea. The tests also evaluated the launcher and its electronics as the company works to develop a maritime strike capability that could be deployed across different classes of vessels. The effort comes as the U.S. Navy looks to expand its use of distributed maritime strike systems, including weapons carried aboard smaller warships and unmanned surface vessels. “Hanwha is answering the U.S. Navy’s call to produce and field modern strike capabilities from a maritime platform,” said Kevin Schoonover, executive vice president for missiles at Hanwha Defense USA. “By pairing Hanwha’s flagship Chunmoo missile and its palletized platform with next generation crewed and uncrewed vessels, we can deliver capabilities for the Navy at scale and a fraction of the cost of other systems.” Schoonover said data collected during the tests would help guide future development of palletized and containerized launch systems for distributed maritime operations and expeditionary strike missions. Unlike permanently installed missile launchers, palletized and containerized systems are designed to provide greater flexibility in how weapons are integrated aboard ships, potentially allowing a wider range of vessels to carry precision-strike capabilities. The demonstration also involved Magnet Defense, which deployed its research vessel to track and evaluate the missile launch. Hanwha Defense USA and Magnet Defense announced a strategic partnership in April to develop and produce medium unmanned surface vessels for the U.S. military. The partnership includes plans for a 38-meter unmanned vessel and the integration of advanced weapons and autonomous systems. The latest missile test could help advance those efforts, although Hanwha has not announced a timetable for operational deployment of the ship-based Chunmoo system. The Spaceport Company, which specializes in offshore launch operations, has conducted more than 10 launches using mobile launch vessels, barges and semi-submersible platforms. Hanwha said its testing program will continue to gather technical and operational data to support the development of maritime strike capabilities for future naval and expeditionary operations. articles.title: Study: Connecting Great Lakes, Inland Waterways Could Deliver Millions in Freight Savings
articles.summary: A new study commissioned by the American Great Lakes Ports Association (AGLPA) identifies opportunities to expand freight movements between the Great Lakes and U.S. inland waterways, potentially delivering millions of dollars in transportation…
articles.body: Study: Connecting Great Lakes, Inland Waterways Could Deliver Millions in Freight Savings Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 17, 2026 Copyright Reimar/AdobeStock A new study commissioned by the American Great Lakes Ports Association (AGLPA) identifies opportunities to expand freight movements between the Great Lakes and U.S. inland waterways, potentially delivering millions of dollars in transportation savings while improving supply chain flexibility and making better use of existing maritime infrastructure. Released November 17, The Great Freight Connection, prepared by transportation consultancy CPCS Transcom Inc., examines existing freight movements between the two systems and evaluates four potential trade corridors involving Port Milwaukee, Ports of Indiana–Burns Harbor and the Illinois International Port District. The findings reveal a significant disconnect between two of America's most important freight networks. In 2023, more than 138 million tons of cargo moved on the Great Lakes and Illinois Waterway systems, yet less than 1% of outbound Great Lakes tonnage moved to the Illinois Waterway. Conversely, approximately 5% of outbound Illinois Waterway cargo moved toward the Great Lakes. Despite their physical connection through Chicago, the systems largely function as separate freight networks. Putting Numbers to the Opportunity The study evaluates four representative trade lanes: grain shipments from Milwaukee to the Gulf Coast, steel from Burns Harbor to Peoria and St. Louis, liquid bulk from Joliet to Milwaukee, and salt moving north from the Gulf to Chicago. Among the most promising opportunities is steel transportation from Burns Harbor to inland markets. The study estimates potential savings of approximately $20.70 per ton for shipments to Peoria and $34.40 per ton to St. Louis compared with trucking. At an illustrative annual volume of 100,000 tons, those savings could reach approximately $2.07 million and $3.44 million, respectively. Moving that volume by water could also eliminate approximately 5,100 truck trips and reduce associated carbon emissions by roughly 87%. Other potential savings include $4.50 per ton for grain shipments, $1.80 for liquid bulk and $19.10 for salt. The figures represent modeled transportation savings rather than guaranteed commercial returns. “Northwest Indiana is home to some of the nation's largest steel producers, and giving them more ways to reach their customers is critical to their success,” said Ryan McCoy, Ports of Indiana–Burns Harbor Port Director. Infrastructure and Commercial Challenges The report identifies several obstacles to expanded cross-system shipping, including limited shipper awareness, established truck and rail relationships, bridge clearance restrictions, aging locks, seasonal navigation constraints and availability of suitable barges. A BNSF railroad bridge near Lemont, Illinois, was identified as a particular operational bottleneck, while lock closures and restrictions on barge movements can undermine service reliability. The study recommends 15 actions covering market development, industry partnerships, regulatory coordination and infrastructure improvements, including expanding lake-capable barge capacity and improving terminal information available to shippers. “By better connecting these systems, we can expand reliable and cost-effective transportation options, strengthen domestic commerce, and create growth opportunities for American industry and workers across America's Heartland,” said Mike McCoshen, Administrator of the Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation. AGLPA and its partners intend to use the findings to engage shippers, carriers and terminal operators in developing commercially viable freight movements. The central conclusion: significant opportunities exist without constructing new waterway connections, provided industry can better utilize those already in place. An Indian seafarer is missing and two others have been hospitalized after the Panama-flagged LPG tanker TARA GAS came under repeated attack in the Strait of Hormuz, forcing its 25-member crew to abandon ship. India’s Ministry of External Affairs said Tuesday that 21 of the 24 Indian nationals aboard had been safely evacuated ashore at Khasab, Oman, while two injured Indian crew members were admitted to a hospital. Search and rescue operations were continuing for the missing seafarer. The latest developments follow two tanker attacks reported Monday by UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) , both of which resulted in engine-room fires. According to UKMTO Warning 208-26 , a tanker was attacked at approximately 1900 UTC on November 16, about seven nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman. The attack disabled the vessel and sparked an engine-room fire. The crew was initially reported safe. However, in an update issued Tuesday, UKMTO said a maritime security agency had reported a second strike against the vessel, causing another fire. At that time, the agency said the crew’s whereabouts were unaccounted for. India’s Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Sarbananda Sonowal, subsequently identified the vessel as TARA GAS , saying it had been targeted in a missile attack on November 16. In a subsequent statement , Sonowal confirmed that the tanker had suffered another attack and its entire crew had abandoned the vessel. “While 24 crew members have been safely accounted for, one Indian seafarer remains missing,” Sonowal said. Video circulating on social media purportedly shows a tanker engulfed in flames near the Strait of Hormuz, although gCaptain has not independently verified the footage. The Indian Embassy in Muscat said it was coordinating with Omani authorities on rescue operations and assistance to the surviving crew. The incident follows a separate attack earlier Monday, when the company security officer of another tanker reported that an unidentified projectile struck the vessel while it was transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz. That incident, recorded under UKMTO Warning 207-26 at 0558 UTC, also caused an engine-room fire. All crew members were accounted for, with no casualties initially reported. The attacks underscore the continuing dangers facing commercial shipping in the strategic waterway, where vessel movements remain severely disrupted by the conflict with Iran. The full extent of the damage to TARA GAS and any potential environmental impact remain unknown. Responsibility for the attacks has not been independently established. articles.summary: Lithuania, Latvia and Germany have submitted an application for a 2 GW hybrid offshore electricity connection that will link the three countries...
articles.body: Interconnectors November 17, 2026 · 1 minute ago 2 GW link between Baltic States and Germany seeking Project of Common Interest status NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Baltic-German PowerLink. Source: Litgrid Lithuania, Latvia and Germany have submitted an application for a 2 GW hybrid offshore electricity connection that will link the three countries to receive EU Project of Common Interest (PCI) status. The 2 GW, 525 kV HVDC Baltic-German PowerLink project is looking to connect the electricity transmission systems of the Baltic States and Germany through a route of approximately 600 kilometers, enabling the integration of around 3 GW of offshore wind capacity in the Baltic Sea region. According to Lithuanian electricity transmission system operator (TSO) Litgrid, receiving PCI status would recognize the project's strategic importance for Europe and create opportunities to access EU funding mechanisms. Litgrid, its Latvian and German counterparts Augstsprieguma tīkls and 50Hertz, submitted the new Baltic-German PowerLink hybrid electricity interconnection project to the ENTSO-E Ten-Year Network Development Plan 2026 (TYNDP) in May 2025. During 2026-2027, the project is in the preliminary study phase, as part of which the three partners are carrying out an initial assessment of the project’s benefits, analyzing alternative connection points in the Baltic States, and evaluating potential financing opportunities. A cost-benefit analysis was also conducted as part of the preparation of the ENTSO-E TYNDP 2026. Upon completion of this process, the project was submitted for inclusion in the next PCI list, Litgrid said. After the preliminary assessments, a decision will be made on whether to proceed to the detailed feasibility study phase. After these studies have been completed, the technical design of the infrastructure will be developed, enabling decisions on the final cost-sharing arrangement and the further implementation of the project. articles.title: Allseas taps Aker Solutions for recycling of 50,000-ton North Sea platform topside
articles.summary: Five decades after a North Sea platform was built, Aker Solutions has been selected to handle the dismantling and recycling of its topside.
articles.body: Project & Tenders November 17, 2026 · 43 minutes ago Allseas taps Aker Solutions for recycling of 50,000-ton North Sea platform topside Five decades after a North Sea platform was built, Aker Solutions has been selected to handle the dismantling and recycling of its topside. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Statfjord A platform in the North Sea Source: Harald Pettersen/Equinor Norway-based energy services provider Aker Solutions has been picked to oversee the final chapter of a 50,000-ton topside from a North Sea offshore platform, taking on its dismantling and recycling in a project that will bring the structure back to the Stord yard, where it was originally built in the 1970s. While announcing a letter of intent (LOI) from Allseas for the reception, dismantling, and recycling of the topside from Equinor's Statfjord A platform in the North Sea, Aker Solutions explained that the platform was originally built at Stord in 1975 and prepared for installation on the concrete gravity base structure in 1976. This platform has been an important contributor to production from the Statfjord field , one of the largest oil fields ever developed in the North Sea. As the original builder of the topside, Aker Solutions elaborates it has detailed knowledge of the structure and extensive experience in maintenance, modification, and life-extension work carried out over several decades. The structure will now return to the yard to complete its life cycle. The LOI for a contract, worth between NOK 0.5 billion ($52 million) and NOK 1.5 billion ($155 million), covers disposal-related preparatory work, reception, dismantling, and recycling of the approximately 50,000-ton topside following offshore removal by Allseas' Pioneering Spirit heavy-lift vessel. Related Articles Decommissioning Allseas books ABL for 60,000-ton topside single-lift ops in next North Sea decom chapter 2 min read " Statfjord A has played an important role in Norway's energy history for almost half a century. We are proud that Allseas and end-client Equinor have selected Aker Solutions to handle the final phase of the topside’s life cycle. The award confirms the strong position we have built in decommissioning and recycling through decades of efficient project execution. " — Guro Rausand Executive Vice President for New Build at Aker Solutions Statfjord A is expected to arrive at Aker Solutions' decommissioning facility at Stord between 2029 and 2031. The dismantling and recycling campaign is expected to take approximately two years. At peak, the project is anticipated to involve around 100 personnel at the Stord yard. " Our decommissioning team has extensive experience in complex offshore decommissioning projects. Combined with our specialized decommissioning facility at Stord, this gives us a strong foundation for carrying out the work safely, efficiently and with a high degree of material recovery. " — Rausand added. The LOI comes shortly after Aker Solutions landed a deal with PTSC Mechanical and Construction Limited Company (PTSC M&C) to handle the multimillion-dollar modernization of an oil field off the coast of Qatar. Based on the DUS OV platform, the vessels are designed for multi-day operations and can be deployed either directly from a port or from an offshore construction (mothership) vessel. Engineering, production and system integration activities are ongoing. According to DEMCON, further updates will follow as the vessels progress towards integration, testing and delivery.
